column2: See the great conches of warriors, the white whisks scattered, the elephants with tongues lolling lying like mountains,
banners variegated, slain elephant-fighters, the coverings of elephants, richly fitted garments and blankets,
varied cloths, caparisons of painted forms, bells broken in many places and crushed by falling elephants,
goads with shafts of lapis lazuli fallen on the ground, golden whips tied to the tips of horsemen's banners,
variegated, jewel-studded and gold-adorned horse-blankets of deer-skin fallen on the ground,
crest-jewels of kings, variegated golden garlands, parasols cast aside, and chowries and fans.
Look at the earth, a mire of blood, covered with the faces of heroes shining like moon and stars, with lovely earrings and trimmed beards, finely adorned.
See, O lord of men, men still alive crying out on all sides, attended by many who have laid down their weapons,
with kinsmen weeping again and again; others, mighty ones, having covered the dead warriors, go again to battle in great fury, eager for victory.
Others, proud, run about here and there, begged for water by their fallen brave kinsmen.
Some who went for water, Arjuna, are lifeless in great numbers; those heroes who returned, seeing them, lost their senses.
Seeing water, they run crying out to one another; see those who have died after drinking and others drinking, O Bharata.
Others, leaving dear ones and kinsmen—friends of kinsmen—were seen departing here and there in the great battle.
See others, best of men, with lips set between their teeth, looking about on every side with faces twisted in frowns.
This deed done by you in the great battle is worthy of you, or of the king of the gods in heaven."
Thus showing the battlefield to Kiritin, Krishna, as he went on, heard a great sound in Duryodhana's army.
The roar of conches and drums mixed with kettledrums and tabors, the noise of chariots, horses and elephants, and the dreadful clash of weapons.
Entering that army with horses swift as the wind, Krishna halted, seeing your army pressed by the Pandya.
That foremost of archers in the battle slew hosts of his foes with various arrows, as Death slays the lifeless.
Piercing with sharp arrows the bodies of elephants, horses and men, that best of strikers made them lifeless.
The Pandya, with arrows, cut the many weapons thrown by the foe's heroes, and slew them, like Shakra the asuras.
[Dhritarashtra said:] Tell me in detail today of the prowess of that hero, his training, power, valour, measure and pride.
[Sanjaya said:] Drona, Bhishma, Kripa, Drona's son, Karna, Arjuna and Janardana—those you deem accomplished in the bow, the best in battle—
he by whom Karna and Bhishma are seen as equal to himself, who does not wish to be less than Vasudeva and Arjuna,
that Pandya, best of kings, foremost of all weapon-bearers, slew Karna's army like Death angered.
That army with its chariots and horses roused, and foot-soldiers and elephants, whirled like a potter's wheel, held by the Pandya.
The Pandya hurled aside foes whose horses, charioteers, banners and chariots were destroyed and weapons thrown away, with well-aimed arrows, as wind scatters clouds.
He slew elephants, whose drivers were struck down, with banners and weapons lost, with their foot-guards, as the destroyer of foes slays foes with a thunderbolt.
He slew those with darts, spears and quivers, horsemen and horses, Pulindas, Khashas, Bahlikas, Nishadas, Dhrakas and Tanganas,
southerners and Bhojas, cruel and rough in battle, and the Pandya deprived them of their weapons and armour with arrows and made them lifeless.
Seeing the Pandya striking down the four-limbed army with arrows in the battle, Drona's son, unperturbed, advanced yet more unperturbed.
Addressing him sweetly, dancing as if fearless, the best of strikers challenged him, smiling first:

O king, lotus-eyed, foremost in weapons and mounts, of thunderbolt frame, renowned for chief strength and manliness,
mahabharata:8:15.14	stretching a great bow with your two long arms, your fists gripping the weapon, you shine exceedingly like a great cloud,
mahabharata:8:15.15	raining down on your enemies with showers of swift arrows; I see no opposing hero to you in battle other than myself.
mahabharata:8:15.16	Alone you crush many chariots, elephants, foot-soldiers and horses, like a fearless, terribly strong lion among herds of deer in the forest,
mahabharata:8:15.17	filling heaven and earth with the great noise of your chariot, like a sudden downpour at the end of the rains making the crops grow.
mahabharata:8:15.18	Touching sharp arrows from your quiver, like venomous serpents, fight with me alone, as Andhaka with the three-eyed one (Shiva).
Thus addressed, saying "So be it" and "Strike!", the Malaya-bannered one, struck by a karnin arrow, pierced the son of Drona.
Drona's son, the best of preceptors, smiling, struck the Pandya with very fierce arrows that pierced vital parts, like tongues of fire.
Then Ashvatthaman loosed nine other sharp iron arrows, feathered with heron plumes, going at the tenth degree of speed.
Of these the Pandya cut five with five sharp arrows, and four killed his horses, which at once lost their lives.
Then, cutting those arrows of Drona's son with sharp arrows, the Pandya, splendid as the sun, cut his stretched bowstring.
Having strung another bow, the foe-slayer, Drona's son, then sent thousands of arrows at the Pandya, making the sky and the quarters thick with arrows.
Then the Pandya, best of men, though knowing those arrows of the great-souled Drona's son to be inexhaustible, cut them all as he shot them.
The foe, having carefully cut the loosed arrows of Drona's son, then drove off his wheel-guards with sharp arrows.
Then, seeing the enemy's quickness, Drona's son, bending his bow into a circle, poured arrows like rain, as Pushan's younger brother pours.
What weapons eight carts yoked with eight oxen could carry, Drona's son hurled in an eighth part of a day, O revered one.
Those who saw him there, enraged like Death, resembling Death at the end of time, mostly lost consciousness.
As the rain-god at the end of summer drenches the earth with its hills and trees, the preceptor's son rained showers of arrows on that army.
The Pandya, the wind, swiftly checked with the Vayavya weapon that irresistible shower of arrows loosed by Drona's son, the rain-cloud, and roared.
As he roared, Drona's son cut his standard adorned with sandal and aguru, like Mount Malaya, and killed his four horses.
Having killed the charioteer, sounding like a great cloud, with one arrow, he cut the bow with a half-moon arrow and shattered the chariot to bits.
Warding off weapons with weapons and cutting all his arms, Drona's son did not kill the foe who had come near, wishing for battle.
Its master slain, the excellent, well-equipped elephant, urged on in haste, strong, going straight—the great lord of the Malaya mounted it, roaring like a lion upon a mountain peak.
The lord of the mountain-kings, roaring, quickly hurled at the preceptor's son a javelin like a sunbeam, pressing his elephant, with effort, anger and great force of arms.
Repeating gladly "He is slain," he shattered the finest ornament of Drona's son, adorned with the best webs of jewels, thunderbolts of gold, silks, garlands and pearls.
That ornament, bright as sun, moon, planet and fire, fell broken by the heavy blow, like a peak of a mountain struck by Indra's thunderbolt on the earth.
Then he blazed with supreme fury, like a king of snakes trodden underfoot, and took fourteen arrows, ender of foes, like Death's rod.
With five he cut the forefeet and trunk of the elephant, with three the king's arms and head, and with six the six chariot-warriors who were followers of the Pandya king, of the finest splendour.
The king's two long, round arms, anointed with excellent sandal and adorned with gold, pearls, jewels and diamonds, fell to the ground, writhing like two serpents struck by Tarkshya.
And his head, with face like the full moon, long reddened eyes in anger and a fine nose, with earrings, falling, shone on the earth like the moon between the two Vishakha stars.

Your sons, surrounded by friends, joyfully honoured greatly the preceptor's son, who had completed his learning and had done his work, as the lord of the immortals honoured Vishnu when Bali was conquered.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "The Pandava is of complete knowledge, strong, disciplined and a hero, permitted over all beings by great-souled Shankara.
From that slayer of foes, Dhananjaya, a great and terrible fear arises. Tell me, Sanjaya, what Partha did there."
[Sanjaya said:] When the Pandya was slain, Krishna said hastily to Arjuna words of benefit: "Look at the greatly honoured king, and the Pandavas who have retreated.
By Ashvatthaman's resolve and by Karna the Srinjayas were slain, and a great slaughter of horses, men and elephants was done." So said the unassailable Vasudeva to Kiritin.
Hearing and seeing this and a great terror for his brother, the Pandava said, "Drive the horses, Hrishikesha, quickly."
Then Hrishikesha went on in his chariot that no foe could withstand, and a dreadful encounter again took place there.
Then the battle between Karna and the Pandavas began again, O best of kings, increasing the realm of Yama.
Bows, arrows, iron clubs, swords, javelins, pattishas, pestles, bhushundis, darts, lances and axes—
With the sound of bowstrings and palms they filled the sky, quarters, intermediate quarters and heaven, and with the rattle of wheel-rims the earth, as they advanced on the foe.
With that great noise, delighted, the heroes engaged in a battle, heroes with heroes, wishing to cross over the end of strife.
The sounds of bowstrings, palms and bows, the trumpeting of elephants and the cries of those struck and falling rose very loud.
Hearing the sounds of arrows and the roaring of heroes, they trembled greatly, struck and fainted, O Bharata.
As they roared and loosed showers of weapons, Karna, Adhiratha's son, crushed many in battle with arrows.
Karna with arrows sent to Yama's abode the chariots of fifteen Panchala heroes with horses, charioteers and banners.
The chief warriors of the Pandus, of great valour, swift with weapons, covered Karna in battle on every side, filling the sky.
Then Karna, churning the enemy army with showers of arrows, plunged into it like a leader of the herd into a lotus-pool full of birds.
Descending into the midst of the foe, Radheya, shaking his excellent bow, struck down their heads with sharp arrows.
Cutting through shields and armour like a fire-offering for embodied beings, no second arrow could bear contact with him.
With arrows loosed from the bow he struck down armour, bodies and lives, with bowstring and guard, as one strikes horses with a whip.
He brought the Pandavas, Srinjayas and Panchalas within range of his arrows; Karna crushed them swiftly, as a lion crushes herds of deer.
Then the sons of the Panchalas, the sons of Draupadi, the twins and Yuyudhana together, O revered one, came at Karna.
Struggling greatly, the Kurus, Pandavas and Srinjayas, giving up their dear lives in battle, went against one another.
Well armoured, wearing mail, with helmets and ornaments, some great chariot-warriors with maces, pestles and iron clubs,
rushed hard at one another like gods with raised rods, roaring, challenging and bounding, O revered one.
Then they struck one another and fell, struck in the battle, vomiting blood from their bodies, with brains and eyes out, in the fight.
With faces like pomegranates, full of teeth and blood, they stood as if alive, supported by their weapons.
Others struck one another with pattishas, swords, darts, bhindipalas, claws, lances and javelins.
Some hewed, others cut, others split, hurled, severed and slew, enraged and pierced through.
Lifeless, they fell, killed by one another, drenched in blood, streaming their own blood like painted sandalwood.
Chariots were destroyed by chariots, elephants by elephants, men by foremost men, horses by horses, by thousands.
Banners, heads, parasols, elephants' trunks and men's arms, cut by razors, broad-heads and half-moon arrows, let go their weapons.
They crushed men, elephants, chariots and horses in the battle; heroes slain by horsemen and elephants with trunks cut off.
With pennants and banners they fell like shattered mountains; elephants and chariots, assailed by foot-soldiers,
were struck and slain on all sides and fell; horsemen, attacked swiftly by foot-soldiers, were killed, and hosts of foot-soldiers slain by horsemen lay in the battle.
The faces of the slain were like crushed lotuses and withered garlands, and their limbs, O wise one,
their forms most desirable, of elephants, horses and men, O king, reached an extreme of dreadful sight, like garments stained.
Easterners and southerners, heroes fighting from elephants, Angas, Vangas, Pundras, Magadhas and Tamraliptakas,
Mekalas, Kosalas, Madras, Dasharnas and Nishadas, skilled in elephant warfare, with the Kalingas, O Bharata,
like clouds raining, with arrows, javelins and iron arrows, they all sprinkled the Panchala mountain in battle.
Wishing to crush those elephants hard with heels, thumbs and goads, the Parshata (Dhrishtadyumna) rained arrows and iron arrows on them, felling them.
He pierced each elephant with ten, six or eight, O Bharata, those mountain-like beasts, with arrows loosed, while being covered by the elephants like the sun by clouds.
The Pandavas and Panchalas, roaring, with sharp weapons, rained on those elephants arrows sounding from the bowstring.
Nakula, Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadi, the Prabhadrakas, Satyaki, Shikhandin and the valiant Chekitana—
the elephants driven by the Mlecchas, with raised trunks, in great fury seized men, horses and chariots and crushed them under foot.
They tore with the tips of their tusks, seizing and hurling, and others, impaled on tusks, fell fearfully.
Satyaki, with a swift iron arrow, pierced the vital part of the Vanga king's elephant moving in front, and felled it.
As he leapt from the elephant, whose driver was thrown, Satyaki struck him in the chest with an iron arrow, and he fell to the ground.
Sahadeva with effort killed, with three iron arrows, the elephant of the Pundra king as it charged, like a moving mountain.
Having made that elephant bannerless, driverless, mailless and lifeless, Sahadeva again approached the Anga king.
Nakula, holding back Sahadeva, struck the Anga's elephant with three iron arrows like Yama's rod and with a hundred more.
The Anga king hurled eight hundred javelins like sunbeams at Nakula, but each was cut into three.
Likewise with a half-moon arrow the Pandava cut his head; the Mleccha king fell slain together with his elephant.
When the preceptor's son, skilled in elephant-training, was slain, the Angas, enraged, with their chief officers came at Nakula on elephants.
With waving pennants in front, golden girths and armour, they swiftly strove to crush him like blazing mountains.
The Mekalas, Utkalas, Kalingas, Nishadas and Tamraliptakas, wishing to kill, loosed showers of arrows and javelins.
As Nakula was covered by them like the sun by clouds, the Pandavas, Panchalas and Somakas rushed up, greatly enraged.
Then took place the fight of chariot-warriors with elephants, loosing showers of arrows and thousands of javelins.
The temples of the elephants burst, and their various vital parts, and the tusks and ornaments of those pierced by iron arrows.
Sahadeva quickly killed eight great elephants with sixty-four sharp arrows; they fell with their riders.
Drawing his excellent bow with effort, using straight-going arrows, Nakula, delight of the Kurus, killed elephants with iron arrows.
Then Shaineya, the Panchalas, the sons of Draupadi, the Prabhadrakas and Shikhandin sprinkled the great elephants with showers of arrows.
Struck by the rain-clouds of Pandava warriors, those mountain-like elephants of the enemy fell by showers of arrows like mountains by showers of thunderbolts.
Having thus slain your elephants, those tiger-like Pandava men watched your army swiftly, like a river with broken banks.
Seeing that army, the soldiers of Pandu's son, having thrown it into confusion again, rushed at Karna alone.
Then, O great king, Duhshasana, a brother, went against his brother Sahadeva, who was enraged and burning your army.
Seeing those two meet in the great fight, the kings there raised lion-roars and waved their garments.
Then, O Bharata, your bowman son, enraged, struck the strong son of Pandu in the chest with three arrows.
Then Sahadeva, O king, pierced your son with an iron arrow and with seventy, and his charioteer with three each.
Then Duhshasana, O king, cutting his bow in the great fight, pierced Sahadeva in arms and chest with seventy-three arrows.
Then Sahadeva, enraged, taking a sword in the great fight, best of fighters, hurled it at your glorious son.
It cut his bow with its bundle of arrows, and then the great sword fell on the ground like a snake fallen from the sky.
Then the valiant Sahadeva took another bow and hurled at Duhshasana an arrow that would end his life.
The Kaurava cut in two with his sharp-edged sword that arrow, as it came, bright as Yama's rod.
Sahadeva, as if laughing, felled with sharp arrows in the battle that sword as it suddenly came.
Then your son in the great battle quickly dropped sixty-four arrows on Sahadeva's chariot, O Bharata.
Those many arrows rushing swiftly, O king, Sahadeva cut one by one with five arrows each.
Having warded off the great arrows sent by your son, Madri's son heaped very many arrows on him.
Then, O great king, enraged, Sahadeva took a dreadful arrow like the Death of the end of time, drew his strong bow and loosed it at your son.
It pierced him with speed, split his great armour and entered the earth like a serpent into an anthill; then, O king, your son, the great chariot-warrior, fainted.
Seeing him dazed, his charioteer, greatly frightened, quickly carried the chariot away as he was struck by sharp arrows.
Having defeated him in battle, the Pandava, younger brother of Pandu's eldest, delighted, crushed Duryodhana's army on every side.
As a man in anger crushes an anthill, O king, so that Kaurava army was crushed by him, O Bharata.
Karna, son of Vikartana, then restrained Nakula, who was impetuous in the fight and tearing the host.
Nakula then said to Karna, laughing: "At long last, gentle one, I am seen by the gods with a kindly eye.
You, evil-eyed, have come within my range in battle; you are the root of all misfortune, enmity and strife.
Through your fault the Kurus have been destroyed, meeting each other; having slain you today in battle, I shall have done my duty and be free of fever."
Thus addressed, the son of the charioteer replied to Nakula, in a manner fitting a prince and especially a bowman:

Strike in battle, boy; let us see your manliness. Having performed your deed in the battle, hero, then you may boast.
mahabharata:8:17.54	Without boasting, dear one, heroes fight according to their strength; fight, and I shall today curb your pride with my power.
Having said this, the charioteer's son swiftly struck the son of Pandu and pierced him in the battle with seventy-three arrows.
Nakula, struck by the charioteer's son, O Bharata, pierced him with eighty arrows like venomous serpents.
Karna cut his bow with thirty stone-whetted arrows with golden feathers and tormented the Pandava, mighty archer.
Piercing his armour, they drank his blood in the battle, as venomous serpents drink water, splitting the earth.
Then taking another formidable bow with a golden back, he pierced Karna with twenty arrows and his charioteer with three.
Then, O great king, Nakula, slayer of heroes, enraged, cut Karna's bow with a very sharp razor-arrow.
Then, smiling, the hero struck him, whose bow was cut, that great chariot-warrior of all the world, with three hundred arrows.
Seeing Karna tormented by Pandu's son, O revered one, the chariot-warriors with the gods were extremely astonished.
Then Karna, son of Vikartana, taking another bow, struck Nakula in the collarbone with five arrows.
With those arrows in his chest, Madri's son shone like the sun spreading light in the world with his own rays.
Nakula, having pierced Karna with seven iron arrows, again cut the tip of his bow, O revered one.
Taking another, swifter bow in battle, he then blocked all quarters for Nakula with arrows.
Suddenly covered by arrows loosed from Karna's bow, that great chariot-warrior quickly cut those arrows with arrows.
Then a net of arrows spread out was seen in the sky, as the sky looks when swarms of fireflies are flying.
The sky was covered by the hundreds of arrows loosed by them, and it was as thronged as with flocks of locusts.
Those golden arrows, falling again and again in rows, shone like swans flying in a line.
When the sky was covered with the net of arrows and the sun hidden, some being then moved, O lord of men.
With their path blocked on all sides by masses of arrows, the two noble ones shone like two newly risen suns.
Though comforted with reasons fixed by the scriptures, he found no peace from the kings, remembering the slaying of the charioteer's son.
The mighty archers, in the grip of rage and indignation, could not bear it; tormented by the king's death, they stood still for a moment.
Why do you grieve, great king? There is no help in grief. Eight and ten akshauhinis have been slain, O lord of men; this earth is now empty, desolate and bare.
Approaching, the great sages, duly honoured, sat on costly seats.
We and Dhritarashtra's sons, subject to the sway of time and anger, having done this blameworthy deed, what fate shall we attain, O king?
And King Dhritarashtra, mighty-armed, sitting near him, the greatly wise, spoke to him who was oppressed by great grief.
The Pandavas used to consult him in all matters, and with his leave they ruled for fifteen years.
Hearing that Vasudeva and Rama had departed, the Pandava gathered his brothers and said, "What shall we do?"
Then, summoning Yuyutsu, Yudhishthira, going forth in search of dharma, handed over the whole kingdom to the vaishya's son.
Then Yudhishthira, seeing Duryodhana, was indignant and suddenly turned back, seeing glory in Suyodhana.
